One of the most important skills in floorball is deciding when to shoot and when to pass.

Most players do not make bad decisions because they do not understand the game. They make bad decisions because everything happens fast. This guide gives you a framework you can use in real time.

This version is ideal for all who want to upgrade their level. The goal is to improve your decision speed without lowering quality.

Core principle: a pass must upgrade the situation

Do not pass just to get rid of responsibility.

Pass only if it clearly improves one or more of these:

  • Shot quality
  • Time on ball
  • Space and angle
  • Number of defenders between ball and goal

If the pass does not improve the attack, shooting is often the better option.

Think in goals, not in actions

The objective in attack is not to pass more. It is to create the next goal.

That means:

  • Shoot when the chance is strong now
  • Pass when the pass creates an even better shot immediately after

Common floorball zones to reference

Use these common zones when evaluating decisions:

  • Slot: central high-danger area in front of goal
  • Half-board: side lane between corner and top area
  • Corner: low side area behind or near goal line
  • Point (top): central top area, farther from goal
  • Weak side: side opposite to where the ball starts

You should usually shoot more from the slot and pass more from low corners or blocked half-board positions, unless a lane opens.

Step 1: Is this a good shot right now?

Use this quick check:

1. Zone

Are you in a dangerous scoring area (for example, in or around the slot)?

2. Shooting lane

Can you get the ball through without a likely block from a defender?

3. Goalie status

Is the goalie moving, screened, or not fully set?

4. Pressure

How close is your defender? Do you have time for a loaded shot, or only a one-touch release?

5. Control

Is your first touch clean enough to shoot with balance and accuracy?

If most answers are yes, shoot.

Read sequence for elite-level speed

Train this sequence until it becomes automatic:

  1. Scan before receiving: goalie, nearest defender, weak-side option
  2. First touch with intent: set up shot or passing lane immediately
  3. Execute in 1-2 touches in dangerous zones

At higher levels, the biggest mistake is delaying the first good option.

Step 2: Is there a better option than shooting?

Now check whether a pass upgrades the situation.

A good pass creates:

  • A clearer shooting lane
  • A better body angle for the receiver
  • A one-touch chance before the defense resets
  • A closer or less contested finish

A bad pass usually does one of these:

  • Moves the ball farther from danger
  • Adds unnecessary touches
  • Gives defenders time to recover
  • Forces your teammate into pressure with poor body position

If the pass does not create a clearly better chance, take the shot.

Fast decision rules you can use in matches

  • Inside slot + clear lane + clean control: shoot immediately.
  • Half-board with blocked lane + weak-side teammate available: pass early.
  • Defender closing hard: one-touch shot or quick release.
  • Goalie out of position: prioritize shooting over extra pass.
  • 2v1 or 3v2 transition: pass only if it creates an open-net or clear one-touch finish.
  • Low corner under pressure: protect ball, then pass to slot or point to re-attack.

Common mistakes

  • Passing to avoid blame instead of attacking to score
  • Taking low-percentage shots from poor angles when a clear upgrade pass is available
  • Overhandling the ball and missing the first good shooting window
  • Forcing highlight passes through traffic

Simple practice ideas

1. 3-second rule finishing

In small-area games, the ball carrier must shoot or create a shot within 3 seconds.

2. Shot or upgrade game

Award points only for:

  • Direct shots from high-danger areas
  • Passes that immediately create a better shot

This trains players to value outcomes, not just ball movement.

3. Video review with two questions

For each offensive clip ask:

  • Was this shot quality high enough?
  • If pass, did it upgrade the chance?
  • Was the decision executed in time, or was the first good window missed?

Final takeaway

Great decision-making is not “shoot more” or “pass more.” It is choosing the action that gives your team the highest chance to score the next goal.

In short:

  • Shoot when the chance is good now.
  • Pass when the pass creates a better chance right away.
fields.Headline: How to improve your decision making (shoot vs. pass)

fields.Page Content:
If your game is built on quick releases, heavy slap shots, and finishing chances under pressure, your stick choice matters.

Shooter-friendly sticks usually share the same profile: fast release, stable blade feel on contact, and enough control to stay accurate at game speed.

Oxdog Hyperlight

The Hyperlight line is a strong fit for players who want a quick release without losing control. It feels light in the hands while still giving enough response in the shaft to generate power.

Why shooters like it:

  • Fast loading and release
  • Easy to shoot off the dribble
  • Reliable for both wrist shots and harder strikes

Best for:

  • Forwards and attacking backs who shoot often and shoot quickly

Oxdog Extremepower

This model is built for players who prioritize shot power. It suits players who like to step into shots from distance and drive through the ball.

Why shooters like it:

  • Strong power transfer
  • Stable feel when loading shots
  • Good option for aggressive shooting profiles

Best for:

  • Players who want heavier shots and more force through contact

Salming Q-Series with Trident Blade

This setup gives a dependable and predictable contact feel. It balances shooting output with control, which is valuable for two-way players.

Why shooters like it:

  • Predictable blade response
  • Good mix of accuracy and power
  • Works well for players who shoot from medium and long range

Best for:

  • Back players who need defensive reliability and shooting threat

Unihoc Carbskin and Unilite Setups

Unihoc lightweight builds with Unilite-style blades are a good fit for technical shooters who rely on timing and placement.

Why shooters like it:

  • Crisp ball feel before release
  • Accurate shooting from multiple angles
  • Lightweight handling for fast preparation

Best for:

  • Technical players who value placement and release speed

Fat Pipe Raw

Raw setups are a solid option for players who want strong shooting without sacrificing overall playability.

Why shooters like it:

  • Good shot authority
  • Stable all-around offensive performance
  • Works for set shots and in-motion finishes

Best for:

  • Players who want power but still need complete offensive utility

How to Choose the Right Shooter Stick

Ask yourself:

  • Do I shoot more wrist shots or more loaded shots?
  • Do I need faster release or more shot weight?
  • Do I need pure offense, or offense plus defensive stability?

Quick guide:

  • Prioritize release speed: Hyperlight
  • Prioritize shot force: Extremepower
  • Prioritize balance and control: Salming Q + Trident
  • Prioritize precision and touch: Unihoc Carbskin/Unilite
  • Prioritize power with all-around offense: Fat Pipe Raw

Final Take

The best stick for shooters is the one that matches how you create shots in real matches.

If your game is based on speed and quick execution, go lighter and faster. If your game depends on distance and heavier contact, prioritize shaft response and blade stability.
fields.Headline: Best Sticks for Shooters
